extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors and other communicators reporting about people with disabilities
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for journalists and communicators on appropriate, respectful, and accurate language when reporting about people with disabilities; includes recommended terminology, contextual notes and Associated Press alignment. Emphasizes asking sources and avoiding stigmatizing wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask sources how they want to be described
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, ask sources how they would like to be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred terminology varies across individuals and communities; asking shows respect and avoids mislabeling. Use the source's stated preference in your reporting when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judgmental descriptors; use 'condition' as substitute
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sensitive when using words like “disorder,” “impairment,” “abnormality” and “special” to describe the nature of a disability. The word “condition” is often a good substitute that avoids judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no universal agreement on terminology; when in doubt prefer neutral phrasing such as “condition.” Avoid language that implies value judgment or pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abnormal/abnormality
rubrics_metrics.description: “Abnormality” can be appropriate in medical contexts (e.g., “abnormal curvature of the spine”), but using “abnormal” to describe an individual is widely viewed as derogatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid calling a person 'abnormal.' Use neutral alternatives like “typical” when comparing; reserve “abnormality” for scientific phenomena or medical test results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afflicted with/stricken with/suffers from/victim of
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like “afflicted with,” “stricken with,” “suffers from” or “victim of” assume the person is suffering or has reduced quality of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer neutral language stating facts about the disability (e.g., “He has muscular dystrophy”). Conforms to AP guidance to avoid descriptions that connote pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Americans with Disabilities Act on first reference; ADA is acceptable on second reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full name on first reference. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amputation/amputee
rubrics_metrics.description: “Amputation” refers to removal of an extremity; people who have undergone amputation are commonly called “amputees,” but the term may be offensive and often is not used correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer phrasing like “someone with an amputation.” Be specific about cause/condition when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autism/autism spectrum disorder/autistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Autism spectrum disorder is a group of complex brain-development disorders with varying symptoms; many experts classify it as a developmental disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having autism only if relevant and you are confident of a medical diagnosis. Ask how individuals prefer to be described (some prefer “autistic,” others “person with autism”). AP: “autism” acceptable as umbrella term; AP does not address use of “autistic” as adjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind/legally blind/limited vision/low vision/partially sighted/visually impaired
rubrics_metrics.description: “Legally blind” denotes visual acuity of 20/200 or less; many with vision loss are not blind. Terms like “low vision,” “limited vision,” or “visually impaired” may be preferable depending on degree of sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use “blind” only for complete loss of sight and “legally blind” for near-complete loss; otherwise ask the source. Note some find “visually impaired” objectionable because it frames condition as deficiency. AP: use “blind” for complete loss and “visually impaired” or “person with low vision” otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brain injury/traumatic brain injury (TBI)
rubrics_metrics.description: TBI is an injury that affects how the brain works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use “person with a brain injury” or “person with a traumatic brain injury” rather than derogatory terms like “brain damaged.” AP: “traumatic brain injury” acceptable in entries about trauma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronic disease/chronic illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Chronic illness refers to health conditions lasting three months or longer and may be lifelong (e.g., diabetes, multiple sclerosis); there is debate about when chronic illness constitutes a disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference a chronic condition only when pertinent and when you’re confident of a medical diagnosis. Ask sources how they want to be described; when in doubt consider people‑first language (e.g., “person with diabetes”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Congenital disability
rubrics_metrics.description: A congenital disability is present since birth and examples include Down syndrome and many forms of cerebral palsy. “Congenital” is not interchangeable with “genetic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable to say someone “has a congenital disability” or “was born with a disability.” State the specific disability when possible. Avoid “defect” or “defective.” AP: “congenital disorder” acceptable; be specific about condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deaf
rubrics_metrics.description: Many do not consider deafness a disability but a culture; people vary in preference between “deaf,” “hard of hearing,” or “partially deaf.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowercase 'deaf' when referring to hearing-loss condition unless the person identifies with the Deaf cultural community and capitalizes it. Use as adjective not noun. Indicate when responses were signed on first reference. AP: uses lowercase 'deaf' for total hearing loss and prefers 'partially deaf' or 'partial hearing loss' for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defect/birth defect
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Defect’ implies imperfection and many find it offensive when applied to people with disabilities; a birth defect is a physical or biochemical difference present at birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'defect' or 'defective' to describe a person; instead state the nature of the disability. AP: 'birth defect' acceptable in broad references but not when referring to a specific person; be specific and use only if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deformed/deformity
rubrics_metrics.description: A deformity denotes atypical body shape and can arise from many causes, but calling a person 'deformed' carries a negative connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'deformed' as an adjective for people. AP medical stories should refer to specific deformities rather than labeling individuals as 'deformed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental disability/disabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Developmental disabilities are conditions arising during the developmental period (manifest before age 22) that often last a lifetime and may require long-term support (e.g., autism, cerebral palsy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While acceptable to use these terms, prefer naming the specific disability when possible. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differently-abled
rubrics_metrics.description: Term originated as an alternative to 'disabled' but is generally not appropriate; some find it condescending or evasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'person with a disability' or be specific about the disability rather than 'differently-abled.' AP: avoid the term and be specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disabled/disability
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Disability’ and ‘disabled’ describe functional limitations affecting major life activities; definitions vary across laws and people with disabilities are not monolithic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid collective labels like 'the disabled.' Do not reference disabilities unless clearly pertinent; when relevant, specify the condition and use people-first language when appropriate. AP: 'disabled' is a general term; avoid 'handicapped.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Down syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is the correct term (not Down’s syndrome in U.S. usage) and is characterized by a range of physical and cognitive traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Down syndrome' and consider people-first language ('person with Down syndrome') or 'has Down syndrome.' Avoid 'suffers from' or 'afflicted with.' If possible be specific rather than using broader labels like 'intellectually disabled.' Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dwarf/little person/midget/short stature
rubrics_metrics.description: Dwarfism is a medical/genetic condition; 'dwarf' can be acceptable medically but often offensive in casual usage; 'midget' is a derogatory slur. 'Little person' and 'short stature' are commonly used; LPA recommends 'short stature', 'little person' or 'someone with dwarfism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only refer to short stature if relevant; ask which term the person prefers. Use 'dwarf' only for medical diagnosis or in quotes; avoid 'vertically challenged' and 'midget.' AP: 'dwarf' preferred term for medical/genetic condition; 'midget' offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic defect/genetic disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Genetic disorder: caused by changes in DNA sequence; examples include cystic fibrosis and sickle cell anemia. A genetic condition is congenital but congenital is not necessarily genetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid terms like 'disorder' or 'defect' when derogatory; use 'condition' and identify the specific diagnosis where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handicap/handicapped
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'handicap' has fallen out of favor among disability communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'handicap' and 'handicapped' when describing a person; instead use the specific condition or 'person with a disability.' The terms may still be used when citing laws, regulations, places or things (e.g., historical signage), though 'accessible parking' is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing impaired/hearing impairment
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms 'hearing impaired' and 'hearing impairment' describe range of hearing loss but many dislike them because they emphasize deficiency; World Federation of the Deaf rejects 'hearing impaired.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'hearing impaired' or 'hearing impairment.' For total hearing loss use 'deaf'; for partial loss use 'partial hearing loss', 'partially deaf', or 'hard of hearing' depending on preference. Ask sources. AP: notes 'hearing-impaired' is not accepted by many deaf and hard‑of‑hearing people.

rubrics_metrics.name: High functioning/low functioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms used to describe ability levels (e.g., 'high functioning autism') are reductive and many find them dismissive or offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'high functioning' and 'low functioning.' Instead use specific medical diagnoses and describe abilities and challenges concretely (e.g., 'lives with minimal or no extra assistance').

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual disabilities/intellectually disabled
rubrics_metrics.description: An intellectual disability involves significant limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both terms are acceptable, but consider people-first language ('person with an intellectual disability') rather than labeling the person. Conforms to AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning disability is a neurologically based condition affecting skills like reading (dyslexia), writing (dysgraphia) or math (dyscalculia); people with learning disabilities typically have average or above-average intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'learning disability' when confident there is a medical diagnosis. If diagnosis is unconfirmed, put the term in quotes and indicate uncertainty. Avoid derogatory substitutes like 'slow learner' or 'retarded.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental illness/mental disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental illness is an umbrella for conditions affecting how people act, think, feel or perceive; terminology is contested due to stigma and some prefer alternative phrasing like 'a person with a psychiatric disorder' or 'mental health experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to mental illness only when relevant and when confident of a medical diagnosis. Specify the illness where possible and always use person-first language. Use quotes and indicate unconfirmed diagnoses when appropriate. Conforms to AP caution against labeling individuals as mentally ill without sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muscular dystrophy (MD)
rubrics_metrics.description: MD refers to a group of more than 30 genetic conditions characterized by progressive muscle weakness; onset varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describing someone as 'someone with muscular dystrophy' or 'someone living with muscular dystrophy' is acceptable; avoid 'suffers from' or 'is afflicted with.' Use MD as acceptable on second reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-disabled
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Non-disabled’ refers to someone who does not have a disability and is preferred in comparative contexts (rather than 'healthy', 'able-bodied', 'normal' or 'whole').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'non-disabled' or 'people without disabilities' when appropriate. Avoid 'able-bodied' except in quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial hearing loss/partially deaf
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Hard of hearing’ is the most common term for mild to moderate hearing loss; 'partial hearing loss' or 'partially deaf' are also used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask sources about preference; otherwise 'hard of hearing' is almost always acceptable. AP recommends 'partial hearing loss' or 'partially deaf' for some usages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient/sick
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing people with disabilities as 'sick' or 'patients' implies they are unwell or in need of medical attention, which may be inaccurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid calling people with disabilities 'sick' or their disability a 'sickness.' Use 'patient' only in medical contexts when the person is receiving medical treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special/special needs/functional needs
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Special needs’ historically described education programs but is now widely considered offensive when describing people; it euphemizes difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'special' and 'special needs' when describing a person or programs except for formal program names or government references. Prefer specific descriptions of disability or 'functional needs' when a term is required. Do not use 'SPED' as shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wheelchair-bound/confined to a wheelchair
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobility equipment is part of personal space and wheelchairs enable mobility; terms like 'wheelchair-bound' or 'confined to a wheelchair' wrongly imply restriction and dependency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe a person as 'someone who uses a wheelchair' and explain why equipment is required if relevant. Avoid 'confined to a wheelchair' or 'wheelchair-bound' because they mischaracterize the role of mobility devices. Conforms to AP style.
